title: "Gemma 4, and Engram's secret ancestor"
date: "2026-04-04"

Google released [Gemma 4](https://huggingface.co/blog/gemma4) this week. Reviewing the architecture, I noticed a familiar mechanism. The smaller models use "Per-Layer Embeddings" (PLE). It looked familiar because DeepSeek's [Engram](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372), submitted six months later, does the same thing.

So are Google copying DeepSeek? No, because [PLE originates in Gemma 3n](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/gemma-3n#ple-caching) released a full six months before Engram.

Engram was billed as "a new axis of sparsity" and "a missing primitive." But the core operation was already known. Google just never wrote the paper!

## The mechanism, side by side

Much of the community's understanding of PLE comes from [antimatter15's reverse-engineering work](https://github.com/antimatter15/reverse-engineering-gemma-3n).

PLE maintains a learned embedding table per transformer layer. At each layer:

1. **Retrieve** a learned vector by token ID.
2. **Gate** via a projection of the hidden state through a non-linearity.
3. **Modulate** by element-wise multiplication.
4. **Inject** back into the residual stream.

Engram performs the same four operations. The difference is the retrieval key: where PLE indexes by single token ID, Engram indexes by hashed N-gram sequence. Set N=1 and the hash reduces to a direct lookup. PLE is the unigram case of Engram.

The remaining differences — which layers carry tables, naming conventions, exact dimensionality — are implementation choices, not architectural ones.

## What Engram genuinely adds

The N-gram generalisation is non-trivial: it requires hashing, collision handling, and vocabulary compression. The sparsity allocation law (20–25% of sparse parameters to memory, the rest to MoE) is a useful empirical finding. The DRAM offloading analysis is practically important. The mechanistic analysis showing the module frees early layers from static pattern reconstruction is illuminating.

DeepSeek are to be applauded for continuing to publish their SoTA research in useful detail. If Google had done the same, maybe they'd have got the citation!
